goals: Relate the shape and bonding of carbon to sp³, sp² and sp hybridisation
Write and read complete, condensed, bond-line and wedge-dash structures
Classify compounds, identify functional groups and name them by IUPAC rules including priority

slides.heading: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles
slides.body_md: Part 1 — carbon forms four bonds and chains, rings and functional groups. We learn to draw, name and distinguish the millions of compounds that result.

visual.alt: Table of four families of organic compounds with an everyday example and key feature

slides.narration: Welcome. Cooking gas, sanitiser, vinegar and the smell of fish are all organic compounds. Carbon atoms join to each other and to a few other elements in countless ways. In this part we study how carbon bonds, how to draw its compounds, how to name them, and how different compounds can share one molecular formula.

slides.heading: Tetravalence and hybridisation
slides.body_md: Carbon has four valence electrons and forms **four covalent bonds** by mixing its 2s and 2p orbitals into equivalent hybrid orbitals. The type of hybrid fixes the **shape**, the **angle** and the **bond length**.

visual.alt: Table of sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation with s character, shape, angle, example and bonds

slides.narration: Carbon forms four bonds because its valence orbitals mix into four hybrid orbitals. With four single bonds, carbon is s p three hybridised and tetrahedral. With a double bond it is s p two and planar, and with a triple bond it is s p and linear. A higher s character pulls electrons closer, so multiple bonds are shorter.

slides.heading: Shapes at carbon
slides.body_md: In **wedge-dash** drawings a solid wedge points towards you and a dashed wedge points away. Multiple bonds shorten the carbon–carbon distance: **154, 134 and 120 pm**.

slides.heading: Four ways to write a structure
slides.body_md: The same compound can be shown at four levels of detail. **Condensed** and **bond-line** formulas save time; **wedge-dash** formulas show 3-D shape.

rows: Zigzag lines; each end or corner is C; H on C omitted
A V shape with OH at the apex
Wedge and dash bonds to OH and H

visual.alt: Table of complete, condensed, bond-line and wedge-dash representations with propan-2-ol as the example

slides.narration: A structure can be written at four levels of detail. The complete formula shows every atom and every bond. The condensed formula writes groups in a line. The bond line formula uses zigzag lines in which each end and corner is a carbon, and hydrogens on carbon are left out. The wedge and dash formula shows the three dimensional shape around a carbon.

slides.heading: Bond-line structures
slides.body_md: To read a bond-line drawing, mark a **carbon at each corner and end**, then add hydrogens until each carbon has four bonds. Heteroatoms such as O are written out, with their H.

slides.heading: Worked example: formula from a bond-line drawing
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the molecular formula of 2-methylbutane drawn as a zigzag of four carbons with a methyl branch on the second carbon.

**Step 1.** Count carbons: 4 in the chain + 1 branch = 5.

**Step 2.** Bonds to other carbons: 1, 3, 2, 1, 1. Hydrogens = 4 minus the bonds on each carbon: 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 $= 12$.

**Step 3.** Molecular formula $\ce{C5H12}$ (alkane $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ with $n = 5$).

visual.alt: Table of the carbon atoms of 2-methylbutane with their carbon-carbon bonds and hydrogen counts

slides.narration: To read the formula, count the carbons first. There are five. Then for each carbon, subtract the number of bonds to other carbons from four to find its hydrogens. The two end carbons and the branch carbon each carry three, the middle carbon carries two and the branch point carries one. The total is twelve, so the formula is C five H twelve.

slides.heading: Classification of organic compounds
slides.body_md: Compounds are first split into **acyclic** (open chain) and **cyclic** (closed ring). Rings are **alicyclic** (behave like open-chain), **aromatic** (benzene-like) or **heterocyclic** (a ring atom other than carbon).

visual.alt: Flow chart of the classification of organic compounds into acyclic and cyclic, with cyclic compounds divided into alicyclic, aromatic and heterocyclic

slides.narration: Organic compounds are first grouped by the shape of their carbon skeleton. Open chain compounds are acyclic. Ring compounds are cyclic, and the rings may be alicyclic, which behave like the open chain compounds, aromatic, which are benzene like, or heterocyclic, which have atoms such as nitrogen or oxygen in the ring. A homologous series is a family that differs by one CH two unit.

slides.heading: Functional groups
slides.body_md: A **functional group** is an atom or group that decides the characteristic reactions of a compound. A **homologous series** has the same group and members differing by $\ce{CH2}$.

visual.alt: Table of eight functional groups with their formula, class and an example

slides.narration: The functional group is the part of a molecule that decides how it reacts. A hydroxyl group makes an alcohol, a carbonyl group at the end of a chain makes an aldehyde and inside a chain makes a ketone, and a carboxyl group makes an acid. Amino, halo and nitro groups complete the common list. Members of a family that differ by one CH two form a homologous series.

slides.heading: IUPAC naming: the basic rules
slides.body_md: **Name = prefix(es) + word root + primary suffix + secondary suffix.** Choose the longest chain containing the functional group, number it from the end giving the **lowest locants**, and list substituents **alphabetically** (di-, tri- are ignored when alphabetising).

visual.alt: Table of the word roots meth to dec for chains of one to ten carbons

slides.narration: An IUPAC name is built from parts. A word root tells the length of the longest chain: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non and dec for one to ten carbons. A suffix names the family, and prefixes name the substituents. Number the chain so the functional group, then the multiple bonds, then the substituents get the lowest numbers, and arrange prefixes alphabetically.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming branched compounds
slides.body_md:
**(a)** $\ce{CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH3}$: longest chain 5 C (pentane), methyl on C2: **2-methylpentane**.

**(b)** $\ce{CH3CH(Cl)CH2CH3}$: butane with Cl on C2: **2-chlorobutane**.

**(c)** $\ce{CH3CH2C(CH3)2CH2CH3}$: pentane, two methyls on C3: **3,3-dimethylpentane**.

In each case the chain is numbered from the end that gives the **lowest locants**.

visual.alt: Table of three branched compounds with parent chain, substituents and IUPAC name

slides.narration: First find the longest continuous chain, then number it from the end that gives the lowest numbers to the branches. The first compound has a five carbon chain with a methyl group on carbon two. The second is butane with chlorine on carbon two. In the third, two methyl groups sit on the same carbon, carbon three, so we write three comma three dimethyl pentane.

slides.heading: Functional group priority
slides.body_md: When a compound has several groups, the **highest-priority group** becomes the suffix and gets the lowest locant; lower groups are named as prefixes. Halo, nitro, alkoxy and alkyl groups are **always prefixes**.

visual.alt: Table of the order of priority of functional groups with suffixes and prefixes

slides.narration: When a molecule has more than one functional group, only the highest priority group is named as the suffix. The order starts with carboxylic acids, then esters, amides, nitriles, aldehydes, ketones, alcohols and amines, with double and triple bonds after these. Any group of lower priority is named as a prefix, such as hydroxy or amino. Halogens and nitro groups are always prefixes.

slides.heading: Worked example: compounds with two groups
slides.body_md:
**(a)** $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2COOH}$: acid outranks alcohol; chain of 4 with COOH as C1: **3-hydroxybutanoic acid**.

**(b)** $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH2OH}$: alcohol outranks alkene; OH gets locant 1: **but-3-en-1-ol**.

**(c)** $\ce{CH3COCH2CH(CH3)2}$: ketone chain of 5 with C=O at 2: **4-methylpentan-2-one**.

visual.alt: Table of three compounds with two groups, the highest-priority group, numbering and name

slides.narration: In the first compound, the acid outranks the alcohol, so the name ends in oic acid and the hydroxyl becomes a prefix on carbon three. In the second, the alcohol outranks the double bond, so the chain is numbered from the hydroxyl end and the name is but three ene one ol. In the third, the ketone gets the lowest number, two, and the methyl is on carbon four.

slides.heading: Rings and aromatic compounds
slides.body_md: Rings take the prefix **cyclo-** (cyclohexane). Substituted benzenes are named as benzene derivatives; two substituents are placed **1,2- (ortho), 1,3- (meta) or 1,4- (para)**. Some common names are retained by IUPAC.

visual.alt: Table of ring compounds and substituted benzenes with formula, name and note

slides.narration: Ring compounds take the prefix cyclo, as in cyclohexane. Substituted benzenes are named as derivatives of benzene. When there are two substituents, their positions are shown by numbers one two, one three and one four, or by the prefixes ortho, meta and para. Several common names such as toluene, phenol and aniline are accepted in the IUPAC system.

slides.heading: Isomerism: same formula, different compounds
slides.body_md: **Isomers** have the same molecular formula but different structures. **Structural isomers** differ in the order of bonded atoms; **stereoisomers** differ only in spatial arrangement.

rows: Place of group or double bond
Different alkyl groups about one functional atom

visual.alt: Table of types of isomerism with the difference and an example of each

slides.narration: Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure. In chain isomers the carbon skeleton differs. In position isomers the functional group or double bond sits at a different carbon. Functional group isomers have different groups, such as an alcohol and an ether. Metamers have different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional atom. Stereoisomers differ only in arrangement in space.

slides.heading: Chain isomers of C₅H₁₂
slides.body_md: Pentane has **three** chain isomers. **More branching, lower boiling point**: the molecule is more compact and has less surface contact for van der Waals forces.

slides.heading: Worked example: isomers of C₄H₁₀O
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Count and classify the isomers of $\ce{C4H10O}$ that are alcohols or ethers.

**Alcohols (4):** butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

**Ethers (3):** methoxypropane, ethoxyethane, 2-methoxypropane.

**Total 7.** Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are **position** isomers; butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are **chain** isomers; butan-1-ol and ethoxyethane are **functional group** isomers; methoxypropane and ethoxyethane are **metamers**.

visual.alt: Table of four pairs of C4H10O isomers with the type of isomerism

slides.narration: The formula C four H ten O fits four alcohols and three ethers, seven isomers in all. Comparing pairs shows the types. The two butanols differ in the position of the hydroxyl, so they are position isomers. Butanol and two methyl propanol differ in the chain. An alcohol and an ether are functional group isomers, and the two ethers with different alkyl groups are metamers.

slides.heading: Stereoisomerism (introduction)
slides.body_md: **Geometrical (cis-trans)** isomers arise when each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups. **Optical** isomers arise at a **chiral carbon** with four different groups; the two forms are non-superimposable mirror images.

slides.narration: Stereoisomers have the same bonding but a different arrangement in space. In cis but two ene both methyl groups are on the same side of the double bond, and in the trans form they are on opposite sides. Lactic acid has a carbon with four different groups, so it exists as two mirror images that cannot be superimposed. We meet these ideas again in later classes.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Carbon is tetravalent: sp³ (109.5°), sp² (120°) and sp (180°); C–C 154, C=C 134, C≡C 120 pm.
Structures: complete, condensed, bond-line and wedge-dash; compounds are acyclic, alicyclic, aromatic or heterocyclic.
IUPAC name = prefixes + root + suffixes; longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical order; highest-priority group is the suffix.
Structural isomers: chain, position, functional group, metamerism; stereoisomers: geometrical and optical.

visual.alt: Summary table of isomer pairs and types

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Carbon forms four bonds using s p three, s p two or s p hybrids. Structures can be written in complete, condensed, bond line or wedge and dash form. IUPAC names follow the longest chain, lowest locants and the priority of functional groups. Isomers may differ in chain, position, functional group or metamerism, and stereoisomers differ in space.

slides.heading: Reactivity, purification and analysis
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how bonds break, why some intermediates are more stable than others, and how chemists purify a compound and find what it contains.

visual.alt: Table of four questions in organic chemistry and the tools used to answer them

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. When an organic molecule reacts, a bond breaks in one of two ways, and the fragments formed are more or less stable depending on electronic effects. We then turn to the practical side: how to purify an organic compound, how to find which elements it contains, and how to calculate its percentage composition.

slides.heading: Fission of a covalent bond
slides.body_md: In **homolytic fission** the shared pair splits evenly, one electron to each atom, giving **free radicals**. In **heterolytic fission** the pair goes to the more electronegative atom, giving a **cation and an anion**.

visual.alt: Table comparing homolytic and heterolytic fission

slides.narration: A covalent bond can break in two ways. In homolytic fission the two shared electrons are divided, one to each atom, giving free radicals. This is favoured by light, heat and non polar solvents. In heterolytic fission both electrons go to the more electronegative atom, giving a positive and a negative ion. This is favoured by polar solvents and polar bonds.

slides.heading: Curved arrows show electron movement
slides.body_md: A **half-headed (fish-hook)** arrow moves one electron; a **full-headed** arrow moves a pair. The arrow starts at the bond or lone pair and ends where the electrons go.

slides.heading: Reaction intermediates
slides.body_md: Bond fission produces short-lived **intermediates**. Their shape follows their hybridisation, and their stability decides which products form.

visual.alt: Table of carbocation, carbanion and free radical with charge, hybridisation, shape and example

slides.narration: Bond breaking gives short lived intermediates. A carbocation has a positive carbon with only six electrons and is flat. A carbanion has a lone pair on a negative carbon and is pyramidal. A free radical has a single unpaired electron and is neutral. Which one forms, and how readily, depends on how well the groups around the carbon can stabilise it.

slides.narration: The tertiary carbocation is the most stable and the methyl cation the least. Each alkyl group pushes electrons towards the positive carbon, and its carbon hydrogen bonds can overlap with the empty orbital, which is called hyperconjugation. The tertiary cation has nine such hydrogens, the secondary six, and the primary three. Free radicals follow the same order, but carbanions follow the opposite order.

slides.heading: Electrophiles and nucleophiles
slides.body_md: An **electrophile** (electron-loving) is electron-deficient and accepts an electron pair. A **nucleophile** (nucleus-loving) is electron-rich and donates a pair. Most organic reactions are a nucleophile attacking an electrophilic carbon.

visual.alt: Table of electrophiles and nucleophiles with the reason for each

slides.narration: An electrophile is short of electrons and accepts a pair. Examples are positive ions, molecules with an incomplete octet such as boron trifluoride, and carbon atoms made partly positive by a polar bond. A nucleophile has a lone pair or a negative charge and donates it. Hydroxide, cyanide, ammonia and water are common nucleophiles.

slides.heading: Inductive effect
slides.body_md: The **inductive effect** is the permanent shift of σ-bond electrons caused by an atom or group, and it **fades quickly with distance**. Groups that pull electrons (−I) include $\text{NO}_2$, CN, halogens; alkyl groups push (+I).

slides.narration: Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so the electrons in the carbon chlorine bond shift towards chlorine. This makes the carbon next to chlorine slightly positive, and it in turn draws electrons from the next carbon, and so on. The effect weakens quickly along the chain and is almost gone by the third bond. Alkyl groups do the opposite and push electrons away.

slides.heading: Resonance: rules and effects
slides.body_md: Resonance structures differ **only in the positions of electrons**, not atoms, have the same number of paired electrons and similar energies. Groups with lone pairs **donate** (+R); groups with multiple bonds to electronegative atoms **withdraw** (−R).

rows: Phenol: O lone pair delocalises into the ring
Ethanoate ion is more stable than the ethoxide ion

visual.alt: Table of resonance effects with groups and example results

slides.narration: In drawing resonance structures only the electrons move, never the atoms, and all structures must have the same number of paired electrons. A group with a lone pair next to a pi system pushes electron density into it, which is the plus R effect. A group with a multiple bond to an electronegative atom pulls density out, which is the minus R effect. Resonance makes a species more stable and equalises bond lengths.

slides.heading: Four electronic effects compared
slides.body_md: **Hyperconjugation** is delocalisation of σ(C–H) electrons into an adjacent empty p orbital or π bond. **Electromeric effect** is a temporary shift of π electrons, only when a reagent attacks.

rows: $\ce{C=O}$ shifts to O when CN⁻ attacks

visual.alt: Table comparing inductive, electromeric, resonance and hyperconjugation effects

slides.narration: Compare the four effects. The inductive effect moves sigma electrons and is permanent. The electromeric effect moves pi electrons, but only at the moment a reagent attacks. Resonance spreads pi electrons and lone pairs and is permanent. Hyperconjugation is the overlap of a carbon hydrogen sigma bond with a neighbouring empty or pi orbital. It is why more alkyl groups make a carbocation or alkene more stable.

slides.heading: Types of organic reactions
slides.body_md: Reactions are classified by what happens to the substrate: **substitution**, **addition**, **elimination** and **rearrangement**. Each can proceed by a radical, nucleophilic or electrophilic mechanism.

visual.alt: Table of types of organic reaction with an example and the mechanism of each

slides.narration: Organic reactions are grouped by what happens to the molecule. In substitution one atom or group replaces another. In addition a molecule adds across a multiple bond. In elimination a small molecule is lost to form a multiple bond. In rearrangement the atoms of the molecule reorganise into an isomer. Each may go by a free radical, nucleophilic or electrophilic mechanism.

slides.heading: Purifying organic compounds
slides.body_md: Choose the method from the **difference in a physical property** between the compound and its impurity.

rows: Different solubility in a hot and cold solvent
Boils lower at low pressure; avoids decomposition
Different solubility in two immiscible solvents
Organic compound from water using ether

visual.alt: Table of methods of purification with the principle and typical use

slides.narration: The method is chosen from a difference in a physical property. Crystallisation uses solubility, sublimation suits solids that turn directly into vapour, and distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Fractional distillation is needed when the boiling points are close. Reduced pressure suits liquids that decompose, and steam distillation suits substances volatile in steam but immiscible with water. Chromatography separates by adsorption or partition.

slides.narration: In thin layer chromatography, spots are applied on a start line and the plate stands in a solvent. The solvent rises, carrying each component a different distance depending on how strongly it sticks to the plate. The Rf value is the distance moved by the spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent front. Matching Rf with pure reference lanes identifies the components.

slides.heading: Worked example: Rf values
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The solvent front moved 8.0 cm. Spot A moved 3.2 cm and spot B moved 5.6 cm. Find the Rf values and say which is more strongly adsorbed.

**Step 1.** $R_f(\text{A}) = \dfrac{3.2}{8.0} = 0.40$.

**Step 2.** $R_f(\text{B}) = \dfrac{5.6}{8.0} = 0.70$.

**Step 3.** A has the lower Rf, so it is **more strongly adsorbed** on the plate.

visual.alt: Table of the distance moved and Rf value of spots A and B

slides.narration: Divide each spot distance by the distance moved by the solvent. For spot A, three point two divided by eight point zero gives zero point four zero. For spot B, five point six divided by eight gives zero point seven zero. The smaller Rf means that A travelled less because it sticks more strongly to the stationary phase.

slides.heading: Lassaigne's test: nitrogen, sulfur and halogens
slides.body_md: Fuse the compound with **sodium metal**, plunge into water and filter: C, N, S and X become $\text{NaCN}$, $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$ and $\text{NaX}$ in the **Lassaigne extract**. $\ce{Na + C + N -> NaCN}$, $\ce{2Na + S -> Na2S}$, $\ce{Na + X -> NaX}$.

rows: Boil with FeSO₄, cool, acidify with conc. H₂SO₄
White (Cl, dissolves in NH₃), pale yellow (Br), yellow (I)

slides.narration: In the Lassaigne test the compound is fused with sodium, which converts the elements into ionic salts that dissolve in water: sodium cyanide, sodium sulfide and sodium halides. Nitrogen gives a Prussian blue colour with iron sulfate and acid. Sulfur gives a black precipitate with lead ethanoate. Halogens are tested with silver nitrate after boiling with nitric acid: white, pale yellow or yellow precipitates show chlorine, bromine or iodine.

slides.body_md: Percentages come from the **mass of a product that contains all of one element**. $m$ is the mass of the compound taken.

slides.narration: Quantitative analysis converts each element into a product that can be weighed or measured. Carbon and hydrogen are found by burning the compound and weighing the carbon dioxide and water. Nitrogen is found by the Dumas method from the volume of nitrogen gas, or by the Kjeldahl method from ammonia. Halogens and sulfur are found by the Carius method as silver halide and barium sulfate, and oxygen is usually found by difference.

slides.body_md: Kjeldahl converts nitrogen to **ammonium sulfate**, then to **ammonia**, measured by titration. Dumas converts nitrogen to **N₂ gas**, measured by volume at STP. Kjeldahl **fails** for nitro, azo and ring-nitrogen compounds.

slides.narration: In the Kjeldahl method, the compound is digested with concentrated sulfuric acid, which turns its nitrogen into ammonium sulfate. Sodium hydroxide then releases ammonia, which is absorbed in standard acid and the unused acid is titrated. In the Dumas method, the compound is heated with copper oxide and the nitrogen gas is collected over potassium hydroxide and its volume is measured at standard temperature and pressure.

slides.heading: Worked example: percentage composition
slides.body_md:
**(a) Liebig.** $0.300\ \text{g}$ of a compound of C, H and O gave $0.660\ \text{g}$ $\ce{CO2}$ and $0.360\ \text{g}$ $\ce{H2O}$. $\%\text{C} = \dfrac{12}{44} \times \dfrac{0.660}{0.300} \times 100 = 60.0$; $\%\text{H} = \dfrac{2}{18} \times \dfrac{0.360}{0.300} \times 100 = 13.33$; $\%\text{O} = 100 - 60.0 - 13.33 = 26.67$. Mole ratio C : H : O = 3.0 : 8.0 : 1, so the empirical formula is $\ce{C3H8O}$.

**(b) Kjeldahl.** $0.40\ \text{g}$ compound; the ammonia neutralised $30.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$. $n(\text{NH}_3) = 2 \times 3.00 \times 10^{-3} = 6.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$, so $\%\text{N} = \dfrac{6.00 \times 10^{-3} \times 14}{0.40} \times 100 = 21.0$.

slides.narration: For the combustion analysis, one twelfth over forty four of the carbon dioxide mass, divided by the sample mass, gives sixty percent carbon, and the water gives thirteen point three percent hydrogen. Oxygen is the rest, twenty six point seven percent, and the mole ratio gives the empirical formula C three H eight O. In the Kjeldahl example, twice the moles of acid gives the moles of ammonia, and the nitrogen is twenty one percent.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Homolytic fission gives free radicals; heterolytic fission gives ions. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃ for carbocations and radicals; the reverse for carbanions.
Inductive (σ, permanent, fades with distance), electromeric (π, temporary), resonance (π and lone pairs) and hyperconjugation (σ C–H).
Reactions: substitution, addition, elimination, rearrangement; electrophiles accept, nucleophiles donate pairs.
Purification matches the method to the property; Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent.
Lassaigne test for N, S, X; Liebig, Dumas, Kjeldahl and Carius for percentages.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Bonds break homolytically to give radicals or heterolytically to give ions, and carbocation stability rises with substitution through inductive effect and hyperconjugation. Resonance and the inductive effect explain acidity and stability. Reactions are classified as substitution, addition, elimination and rearrangement. Purification methods are matched to a property, and Lassaigne and quantitative tests reveal composition.

sections.heading: 1. Tetravalence, hybridisation and structural representations
sections.body_md:
Carbon (1s² 2s² 2p²) forms **four covalent bonds** by promoting an electron and mixing orbitals. **sp³**: four σ bonds, tetrahedral, 109.5° (C–C 154 pm in ethane). **sp²**: three σ and one π, trigonal planar, 120° (C=C 134 pm in ethene). **sp**: two σ and two π, linear, 180° (C≡C 120 pm in ethyne). The higher the s character (25%, 33%, 50%), the shorter and stronger the bond.

Structures are written as **complete** (all atoms and bonds), **condensed** ($\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH3}$), **bond-line** (each end or corner is C; H on C omitted; heteroatoms written out) and **3-D wedge-dash** (solid wedge towards the viewer, dashed away). Count hydrogens as 4 minus the bonds on each carbon.

key_terms.definition_md: Mixing of atomic orbitals of one atom to form equivalent hybrid orbitals.
A zigzag drawing in which every end and corner is a carbon atom.

sections.heading: 2. Classification and IUPAC nomenclature
sections.body_md:
**Acyclic** (open chain) and **cyclic** compounds; cyclic ones are **alicyclic**, **aromatic** (benzenoid or non-benzenoid) or **heterocyclic**. A **functional group** gives characteristic reactions; a **homologous series** has the same group and members differing by $\ce{CH2}$.

**IUPAC name** = prefix + word root + primary suffix (-ane, -ene, -yne) + secondary suffix. Word roots: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non, dec. Rules: longest chain containing the principal group; lowest locants (group, then multiple bonds, then substituents); alphabetical prefixes; di-, tri- ignored in alphabetising.

**Priority** (high to low): carboxylic acid, ester, acid halide, amide, nitrile, aldehyde, ketone, alcohol, amine, alkene, alkyne. Halo, nitro, alkoxy and alkyl are only prefixes. Examples: 2-methylpentane, 3-hydroxybutanoic acid, but-3-en-1-ol, 4-methylpentan-2-one, 3,3-dimethylpentane.

key_terms.definition_md: An atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic chemical properties of a compound.
The number that shows the position of a substituent or group on the chain.

sections.heading: 3. Isomerism
sections.body_md:
**Structural isomers** (same molecular formula, different connectivity): **chain** (butane / 2-methylpropane), **position** (propan-1-ol / propan-2-ol), **functional group** (ethanol / methoxymethane) and **metamerism** (methoxypropane / ethoxyethane). $\ce{C5H12}$ has three chain isomers; branching lowers the boiling point (309, 301, 283 K). $\ce{C4H10O}$ has seven alcohol and ether isomers.

**Stereoisomers** (same connectivity, different arrangement in space) are only introduced: **geometrical** (cis and trans but-2-ene; each C=C carbon needs two different groups) and **optical** (a chiral carbon bonded to four different groups gives non-superimposable mirror images, as in lactic acid).

key_terms.definition_md: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.
A carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups.

sections.heading: 4. Bond fission, intermediates, electrophiles and nucleophiles
sections.body_md:
**Homolytic fission**: one electron to each atom, **free radicals** (half-headed arrows; light, heat, non-polar solvent). **Heterolytic fission**: both electrons to the more electronegative atom, **ions** (full arrow; polar solvent).

**Carbocation** (sp², planar, six electrons), **carbanion** (sp³, pyramidal, lone pair), **free radical** (one unpaired electron). Stability: carbocations and radicals $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{CH}_3$; carbanions the reverse. **Electrophiles** accept an electron pair ($\ce{H+}$, $\ce{NO2+}$, $\ce{BF3}$, carbonyl carbon); **nucleophiles** donate one ($\ce{OH-}$, $\ce{CN-}$, $\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{H2O}$).

key_terms.definition_md: A species with an unpaired electron, formed by homolytic fission.
An electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair.
An electron-rich species that donates an electron pair.

sections.heading: 5. Electronic displacements
sections.body_md:
**Inductive effect**: permanent shift of σ electrons along a chain; −I groups ($\ce{NO2}$, CN, F, Cl, Br, I, OH) and +I groups (alkyl, increasing from CH₃ to tert-butyl); it fades with distance. It explains why Cl₃CCOOH (pKa about 0.7) is far stronger than CH₃COOH (about 4.8).

**Electromeric effect**: temporary shift of π electrons only in the presence of an attacking reagent. **Resonance**: delocalisation of π electrons and lone pairs; structures differ only in electron positions and have the same number of paired electrons; the **hybrid** is more stable (benzene: all C–C 139 pm; carboxylate: equal C–O bonds). **+R**: –OH, –OR, –NH₂, –X; **−R**: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH. **Hyperconjugation**: delocalisation of σ(C–H) electrons into an adjacent p orbital or π bond; the more α hydrogens, the more stable (ethyl 3, isopropyl 6, tert-butyl 9).

key_terms.definition_md: Permanent polarisation of a σ bond caused by an electronegative or electropositive group.
Delocalisation of electrons that makes the real structure a hybrid of several contributing structures.
Delocalisation of electrons of a σ(C–H) bond into an adjacent empty p orbital or π bond.

sections.heading: 6. Types of reactions and purification
sections.body_md:
**Substitution** ($\ce{CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl}$, radical; $\ce{CH3Br + OH- -> CH3OH + Br-}$, nucleophilic; nitration of benzene, electrophilic), **addition** ($\ce{C2H4 + HBr -> C2H5Br}$, electrophilic; $\ce{CH3CHO + HCN -> CH3CH(OH)CN}$, nucleophilic), **elimination** ($\ce{C2H5Br + KOH -> C2H4 + KBr + H2O}$) and **rearrangement** ($\ce{NH4CNO -> (NH2)2CO}$).

**Purification:** crystallisation (solubility); sublimation (naphthalene, camphor); simple distillation (boiling points differ considerably: chloroform 334 K, aniline 457 K); fractional distillation (close boiling points: acetone 329 K, methanol 338 K); distillation under reduced pressure (glycerol); steam distillation (aniline); differential extraction (ether); **chromatography** (adsorption: column, TLC; partition: paper). $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the spot}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent front}}$, always less than 1.

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio of the distance moved by a component to the distance moved by the solvent front.
Distillation of a substance that is volatile in steam and immiscible with water, at a temperature below its boiling point.

sections.heading: 7. Qualitative and quantitative analysis
sections.body_md:
**Lassaigne extract** (fuse with sodium, extract in water): $\ce{Na + C + N -> NaCN}$, $\ce{2Na + S -> Na2S}$, $\ce{Na + X -> NaX}$. **N:** boil with FeSO₄, acidify with conc. H₂SO₄: Prussian blue. **S:** lead ethanoate gives black PbS; sodium nitroprusside gives violet. **N and S:** blood-red with FeCl₃. **Halogens:** boil with HNO₃ (removes CN⁻, S²⁻), add AgNO₃: white (Cl, soluble in NH₃), pale yellow (Br, sparingly soluble), yellow (I, insoluble).

**Percentages:** Liebig, $\%\text{C} = \tfrac{12}{44}\tfrac{m_{\text{CO}_2}}{m} \times 100$ and $\%\text{H} = \tfrac{2}{18}\tfrac{m_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}}{m} \times 100$. Dumas, $\%\text{N} = \tfrac{28 V}{22400\,m} \times 100$ ($V$ in mL at STP). Kjeldahl, $\%\text{N} = \tfrac{1.4NV}{m}$ (fails for nitro, azo and ring N). Carius: $\%\text{X} = \tfrac{\text{atomic mass}}{\text{M of AgX}}\tfrac{m_{\text{AgX}}}{m} \times 100$; $\%\text{S} = \tfrac{32}{233}\tfrac{m_{\text{BaSO}_4}}{m} \times 100$; $\%\text{P} = \tfrac{62}{222}\tfrac{m_{\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7}}{m} \times 100$; oxygen by difference.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Choosing the longest chain without the principal functional group, or numbering for substituents before the group.
- Calling any pair of isomers "chain isomers" without checking skeleton, position, group and alkyl groups.
- Putting carbanions in the carbocation stability order.
- Using a full arrow for one electron, or an arrow that starts at the wrong place.
- Forgetting the nitric acid boil before silver nitrate in the halogen test.
- Using the wrong factor (12/44, 2/18, 32/233) or forgetting that Rf is below 1.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: hybridisation, functional group, IUPAC name, type of fission, colour of a test.
- 2–3 marks: explanation with the effect named (+I, −R, hyperconjugation) and a clear conclusion; curved arrows.
- Numericals: formula (1), substitution (1), answer with units or percentage (1).

questions.stem_md: Explain the four kinds of structural isomerism, with one example of each. Name the two kinds of stereoisomerism.

Functional group isomers contain different groups, as in ethanol and methoxymethane. Metamers have different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional atom, as in methoxypropane and ethoxyethane. Stereoisomerism is of two kinds: geometrical (cis-trans) and optical.

questions.stem_md: Chloroethanoic acid has a pKa of about 2.9, whereas ethanoic acid has a pKa of about 4.8. Explain this difference.

answer.model_answer_md: Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon and pulls electrons along the σ bonds (−I effect). questions.solution_md: −I effect of Cl stabilises the anion.

questions.stem_md: Define electrophile and nucleophile, giving two examples of each.

answer.model_answer_md: An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair, for example $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{BF3}$. A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to a positive centre, for example $\ce{OH-}$ and $\ce{NH3}$.

questions.stem_md: All six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are 139 pm long, although the Kekulé structure shows three single and three double bonds. Explain this, and say what the resonance energy implies.

answer.model_answer_md: Benzene is not described by either Kekulé structure alone. The real molecule is a resonance hybrid of the two, in which the six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, so every carbon–carbon bond is equal in length, between a single bond (154 pm) and a double bond (134 pm). The hybrid is more stable than either contributing structure, and the resonance energy measures this extra stability.

questions.solution_md: Hybrid of two structures; delocalised π electrons; extra stability.

questions.stem_md: Use hyperconjugation to explain why the isopropyl cation $(\ce{CH3})_2\ce{CH+}$ is more stable than the ethyl cation $\ce{CH3CH2+}$.

answer.model_answer_md: In hyperconjugation the electrons of an α C–H σ bond are delocalised into the empty p orbital of the positive carbon, which spreads the charge. The ethyl cation has one methyl group with three α C–H bonds, so it has three hyperconjugative structures. The isopropyl cation has two methyl groups and six α C–H bonds, so it has six structures, a greater delocalisation, and is more stable.

questions.solution_md: Three versus six α C–H bonds.

questions.stem_md: Explain the inductive effect, the resonance effect and hyperconjugation, with one example of each, and state which of them is temporary.

answer.model_answer_md: The inductive effect is the permanent shift of σ electrons caused by an electronegative group; in 1-chlorobutane the C–Cl bond is polarised and the effect fades along the chain. The resonance effect is the delocalisation of π electrons or lone pairs, as in benzene or the ethanoate ion, where all C–O bonds become equal. Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of σ(C–H) electrons into an adjacent p orbital or π bond, which makes a tertiary carbocation more stable than a primary one. All three are permanent; the temporary effect is the electromeric effect.

questions.solution_md: Three effects with examples; electromeric is temporary.

**(a)** (b) The positive carbon is sp² hybridised and the cation is planar

**(b)** Three methyl groups: nine.

**(c)** (i) More stable tertiary cation: +I and hyperconjugation.

(ii) Methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary.

questions.stem_md: Describe (a) fractional distillation, (b) steam distillation and (c) differential extraction, giving the principle and one use of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Fractional distillation separates liquids with close boiling points, such as acetone and methanol; a fractionating column provides repeated vaporisation and condensation, so the more volatile liquid collects first. (b) Steam distillation purifies a substance that is volatile in steam and immiscible with water, such as aniline; it distils below its own boiling point with the steam. (c) Differential extraction uses two immiscible solvents: an organic compound in water is shaken with ether, in which it is more soluble, and the ether layer is separated and evaporated.

questions.stem_md: Describe the principle of the Dumas method and of the Kjeldahl method for estimating nitrogen. Write the formula for the percentage of nitrogen in each, and give one limitation of the Kjeldahl method.

In the Kjeldahl method, the compound is digested with concentrated sulfuric acid to give ammonium sulfate; sodium hydroxide releases ammonia, which is absorbed in standard acid and the unused acid is titrated, so $\%\text{N} = \dfrac{1.4NV}{m}$. Kjeldahl does not work for nitro, azo and ring nitrogen.

questions.stem_md: In a Kjeldahl estimation, the ammonia from $0.350\ \text{g}$ of a compound neutralised $20.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ (N = 14). Calculate the percentage of nitrogen.
questions.solution_md: $n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) = 0.200 \times 20.0/1000 = 4.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$. Each H₂SO₄ neutralises 2 NH₃, so $n(\text{N}) = 8.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ and $\%\text{N} = \dfrac{8.00 \times 10^{-3} \times 14}{0.350} \times 100 = 32.0$.

questions.stem_md: $0.300\ \text{g}$ of an organic bromine compound, heated with fuming nitric acid and silver nitrate (Carius method), gave $0.376\ \text{g}$ of silver bromide (Br = 80, Ag = 108). Calculate the percentage of bromine.
questions.solution_md: Molar mass of AgBr $= 108 + 80 = 188$. $\%\text{Br} = \dfrac{80}{188} \times \dfrac{0.376}{0.300} \times 100 = 53.33$, so 53.3% of bromine.

questions.stem_md: $0.200\ \text{g}$ of an organic sulfur compound gave $0.466\ \text{g}$ of barium sulfate (Ba = 137, S = 32, O = 16). Calculate the percentage of sulfur.
questions.solution_md: Molar mass of $\text{BaSO}_4 = 137 + 32 + 64 = 233$. $\%\text{S} = \dfrac{32}{233} \times \dfrac{0.466}{0.200} \times 100 = 32.00$, so 32.0% of sulfur.

questions.stem_md: A compound has $R_f = 0.350$ in a solvent system. In an experiment the solvent front moved $12.0\ \text{cm}$ from the start line. How far, in cm, did the compound's spot move?
questions.solution_md: $R_f = \dfrac{d_\text{spot}}{d_\text{solvent}}$, so $d_\text{spot} = 0.350 \times 12.0 = 4.20\ \text{cm}$.

questions.stem_md: A compound contains 54.5% C, 9.1% H and 36.4% O (given) and has a molar mass of 88 g mol⁻¹. Find the number of hydrogen atoms in a molecule of the compound.
questions.solution_md: Moles per 100 g: C $= 54.5/12 \approx 4.54$; H $= 9.1/1 = 9.1$; O $= 36.4/16 \approx 2.27$. Dividing by the smallest value, 2.27, gives the ratio C : H : O = 2 : 4 : 1, so the empirical formula is $\ce{C2H4O}$ with mass 44. Then $n = 88/44 = 2$, so the molecular formula is $\ce{C4H8O2}$ and the number of hydrogen atoms is $4 \times 2 = 8$.
